title: Huma Qureshi Doesn't Speak a Single Word in Her New Film. It Might Be the Most Dangerous Performance of the Year.
excerpt: Baby Do Die Do introduces Bollywood's first deaf-mute professional hitwoman — and she's releasing the same day as Alia Bhatt's Alpha. July 3 just got very interesting.
body:
There's a woman with a red umbrella walking through a Mumbai crowd. She moves the way the city moves — unhurried, anonymous, swallowed whole by the chaos of bodies and noise. And then someone dies. And she's already gone.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=YXPVEtFCb9s</youtube>

That's the image at the centre of the **Baby Do Die Do** teaser, which dropped this week and immediately established itself as one of the most visually arresting promos Bollywood has produced in 2026. **Huma Qureshi** plays **Baby KarMarKar** — an NGO worker for the differently abled who moonlights, with chilling precision, as a contract killer on Mumbai's streets. The catch? Baby is both deaf and mute. She doesn't speak. She doesn't hear. She kills, and she vanishes into the gardi.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZWuqRlABdT/

Let that sink in for a moment. This is the first time Hindi cinema has given us a professional female assassin as the lead. Not a woman forced into violence by circumstance. Not a revenge arc. A professional. One who happens to navigate a world designed entirely around sound — without access to any of it.

## A Performance Without Words

Director **Nachiket Samant**, who previously directed Huma in *Single Salma*, has spoken candidly about the film's most audacious creative decision: stripping his lead actor of all dialogue.

> "Huma's a fully tayyar actor, but this time, suddenly taking away her dialogues seemed like the perfect challenge. It forced her somewhere I hadn't seen her go, and she rose to it completely." — Nachiket Samant

The entire film rests on Huma's physical presence — her body language, her gaze, the way she holds that umbrella like it might be something else entirely. It's the kind of performance gamble that either collapses into gimmick or ascends into something unforgettable. Based on the teaser, the odds look very good.

The idea, Samant says, emerged from a disarmingly simple question: has there ever been a Hindi film about a professional female assassin? "We couldn't think of one. That gap was instantly exciting, so we went after that character, and the world kind of built itself around her."

## Mumbai as Accomplice

What makes Baby lethal isn't just skill — it's geography. Mumbai's density, its suffocating crowds, its refusal to stop for anything or anyone. Baby kills and disappears into the multitude. "It's as much about the escape as it is about the kill," Samant explained. The film's rap anthem 'Gardi,' penned by **WB Sam** and composed by **Arjun Iyer**, captures this spirit — the thrum and crush of a city that swallows secrets whole.

The supporting cast adds texture. **Seema Pahwa** plays a police inspector who's more amused than alarmed by the emergence of a new killer in her jurisdiction — a delicious character beat. **Sikander Kher**, **Chunky Panday**, **Rachit Singh**, and **Vidya Malavade** round out what promises to be a rich ensemble of Mumbai's morally compromised. The story itself comes from **Jasmeet K Reen**, who wrote *Darlings* — a pedigree that suggests Baby Do Die Do won't shy away from the darker corners of its premise.

Producer **Saqib Saleem** — Huma's brother — is backing the film under the Saleem Siblings banner in association with Pune 04 Films. Family enterprise, intimate budget, massive swing.

## The July 3 Collision

Here's where it gets interesting. Baby Do Die Do releases on **July 3, 2026** — the exact same date as **Alpha**, the YRF Spy Universe's first female-led instalment starring **Alia Bhatt** and **Sharvari Wagh**. Two films about women who are trained to kill. One is a ₹200-crore-plus franchise spectacle with the biggest female star in the country. The other is a scrappy indie noir where the lead actress doesn't say a word.

It's the kind of clash that feels less like scheduling conflict and more like a referendum on what Bollywood audiences actually want from their action heroines in 2026. The polished, universe-building, teaser-driven machine of YRF — or the stripped-down, Mumbai-soaked, character-first gamble of a film where the weapon is a red umbrella and the protagonist communicates in silence.

For diaspora audiences, both films will play in theaters across North America, the UK, and the Gulf. If you're choosing between the two on opening weekend — and you probably will be — the question isn't which one has the bigger budget. It's which one has something to say.

Our money's on the woman who doesn't need words to make you listen.
